enum: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies
JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies

raw_response.chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Can't tell / Not applicable (cross-sectional survey design with no longitudinal follow-up; however, although sample size estimation assumed a 5 per cent non-response rate, actual household refusal and non-response counts during purposive/snowball recruitment are not reported).
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern (comparisons of water, sanitation, drainage, housing, and electricity across notified slums, non-notified slums, and open spaces rely solely on unadjusted bivariate chi-square tests with no measurement or statistical control for household income, exact migration duration within the 30-day to 10-year window, caste/state of origin, rental vs. ownership tenure, or settlement age).
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Moderate concern / Adequate with limitations (slum notification status is anchored in the official 2009 Municipal Corporation of Ludhiana list reflecting the 1986 statutory notification and Census of India 2011 definitions, and voter/ration card possession and metered vs. street-tapped electricity are recorded; however, combining municipally 'recognized' slums slated for phased service provision with unrecognized 'identified' slums into a single 'non-notified' category obscures an important administrative distinction, MCL's underlying slum inventory dropped inexplicably from 209 slums in 2007 to 91 in 2009, and legal vs. unauthorized piped water connections were not differentiated).
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Moderate concern / Unclear (data were collected from heads of households using an undescribed survey instrument with no reported validation, pre-testing, interviewer training, or direct physical verification of facilities; notably, the survey failed to distinguish formal from illegal piped water connections despite the authors noting widespread unauthorized water tapping across Ludhiana).
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate concern (water supply source, drainage type, defecation facility, electricity connection, and NSS/Census housing structure categories are clearly defined, but rely on unvalidated household-head self-report without water quality testing, formal vs. illegal water connection differentiation, or sanitary inspection of latrines).
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Some concern (Section III.g states that odds ratios and 95 per cent confidence intervals were calculated where appropriate, yet none are reported anywhere in the paper; furthermore, reported degrees of freedom in Tables 3 and 4 [df = 6, 2, 6, 4, 4] contradict Footnote 2 stating that 'Open spaces' was collapsed with 'Non-notified slums' for chi-square testing).
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: High concern (while 15 notified and 15 non-notified slums were selected via simple random sampling from the 2009 MCL slum list, household selection within clusters relied on non-probability purposive and snowball sampling, targeted newer slums/camps, included 30 households in 'open spaces' outside the formal cluster frame, and omitted actual refusal/response rates).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the criteria for inclusion in the sample clearly defined?
domain_ratings.justification: Eligibility criteria were explicitly defined: consenting 'newer migrant' households that had migrated to Ludhiana more than 30 days ago and less than 10 years ago, residing in the selected slum settlements, while excluding recent (<30 days) and older (>=10 years) migrants.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section III & Section III.b, PDF Pages 4–5

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the study subjects and the setting described in detail?
domain_ratings.justification: The Ludhiana urban-industrial setting, municipal slum inventory, data collection period (1 August 2011–31 July 2014), cluster household totals, housing tenure, and voter/ration card possession are well described, but basic sociodemographic characteristics of the 3,947 sampled households (age, sex, income, occupation, education, state of origin proportions, and distribution of stay duration) are completely omitted.
domain_ratings.where_found: Sections II.a, III, III.c & IV (Tables 1–3), PDF Pages 3–8

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the exposure measured in a valid and reliable way?
domain_ratings.justification: Slum legal status ('notified' vs. 'non-notified') was classified using the official Municipal Corporation of Ludhiana (MCL) 2009 list of 50 notified and 41 non-notified slums and Census of India 2011 definitions, though merging municipally 'recognized' slums (eligible for phased municipal provision) with 'identified' slums under 'non-notified' introduces administrative heterogeneity and MCL's benchmark counts showed prior inconsistency (209 slums in 2007 vs. 91 in 2009).
domain_ratings.where_found: Sections II.a, III & III.f, PDF Pages 3–6

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were objective, standard criteria used for measurement of the condition?
domain_ratings.justification: Standard Census of India 2011 operational definitions were applied for notified, recognized, and identified slums, Open Government Data / National Sample Survey criteria were used to classify pucca, semi-pucca, and katcha housing, and explicit residency thresholds (>30 days to <10 years) defined newer migrant status.

Key potential confounders of the association between slum notification status and household civic amenities—such as household income/wealth, exact duration of residence in Ludhiana, caste/origin, and settlement age—were neither identified in the design nor measured; rental tenure is discussed only post-hoc to explain higher pucca housing prevalence.
domain_ratings.where_found: Sections III, IV (Table 2) & V, PDF Pages 4–8, 11

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were strategies to deal with confounding factors stated?
domain_ratings.justification: No design or analytical strategies (such as multivariable regression, stratification, or restriction/matching on tenure or socioeconomic status) were stated or used to address confounding; all comparisons across slum categories are unadjusted bivariate tabulations.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section III.g & Section IV (Tables 3–4), PDF Pages 6, 8–9

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the outcomes measured in a valid and reliable way?
domain_ratings.justification: Civic amenity outcomes were gathered from household heads using a survey, but the paper reports no details on instrument validation, pilot testing, interviewer training, or direct observational verification of sanitation/water infrastructure, and the authors acknowledge that formal vs. unauthorized piped water connections were not distinguished.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section III.e & Section V, PDF Pages 5, 9–11

domain_ratings.justification: Statistical analysis relied on naive Pearson chi-square tests that failed to account for cluster-level intraclass correlation across the 30 slum clusters (despite assuming a design effect of 1.7 in sample size calculation) or snowball recruitment dependence; reported degrees of freedom in Tables 3 and 4 (df = 6, 2, 6, 4, 4) contradict Footnote 2 stating that 'Open spaces' was combined with 'Non-notified slums' into a two-group comparison; and odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals promised in Section III.g are omitted entirely.
domain_ratings.where_found: Sections III.a, III.g & IV (Tables 3–4), PDF Pages 4–6, 8–9

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: This analytical cross-sectional survey of 3,947 newer migrant households across 15 notified slums, 15 non-notified slums, and open spaces in Ludhiana, North India (2011–2014) is judged to be of High concern on the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies (Yes: Q1, Q3, Q4; Unclear: Q2, Q7; No: Q5, Q6, Q8). Strengths include clear migration-duration inclusion criteria (30 days to 10 years), random first-stage selection of 15 notified and 15 non-notified slum clusters from Municipal Corporation of Ludhiana lists, and standard Census/NSS definitions for slum and housing categories. However, internal validity and comparative inference between notified and non-notified settlements are substantially weakened by: (1) non-probability purposive and snowball recruitment of households within clusters without reporting non-response rates; (2) absence of demographic/socioeconomic sample descriptors and complete lack of measurement or statistical adjustment for confounders (such as income, duration of stay, and rental vs. owner tenure); (3) unvalidated household-head survey measurement that could not separate formal from unauthorized piped water connections and grouped municipally 'recognized' slums with unrecognized 'identified' slums; and (4) flawed statistical analysis using unadjusted chi-square tests that ignore cluster correlation, exhibit internal degrees-of-freedom contradictions in Tables 3 and 4, and omit the odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals stated in the Methods.
raw_response.study_design_identified: Analytical cross-sectional household survey (two-stage sampling: simple random sample of 15 notified and 15 non-notified slum settlements, followed by purposive and snowball sampling of 3,947 newer migrant households comparing civic amenities across slum legal notification categories)
raw_response.where_found_summary: Abstract (PDF Page 1); Section II & II.a Aims, Objectives and Background (PDF Pages 2–4); Section III Materials and Methods, subsections a–g, and Table 1 (PDF Pages 4–6); Section IV Observations and Results and Tables 2–4 (PDF Pages 7–9); Section V Discussion and Table 5 (PDF Pages 8–13); Section VI Conclusions (PDF Page 13).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The study is a quantitative cross-sectional household survey collected at a single point in time per household (2011–2014) that statistically compares water supply, sanitation, drainage, housing, electricity, and identity card outcomes across administrative slum categories (notified slums, non-notified slums, and open spaces) using chi-square tests, with no randomized assignment and no quasi-experimental intervention/policy evaluation design (no longitudinal panel, pre-post comparator, DiD, IV, RDD, or matching). Accordingly, the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies is the exact matching appraisal tool.
